name: Daria Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. Tell me about your factory work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a carpet-tufting machine. Yarn feeds through the needles into backing, and I check the pile height and stop the machine when a needle misses. I have a vocational textile certificate and several years on the floor, doing a decent ordinary job. The wage is low for an experienced operator, and this is one of the few textile plants within travelling distance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do things look at home and with new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Joel cooks at a small café; our children are grown and have their own households. We rent and have about three weeks of expenses saved. I like to learn from someone who already knows a machine, and I use AI now and then to explain a maintenance word before checking the printed manual. I would try a proven new control, but not on a live carpet run without a proper demonstration. We talk about leaving full-time shifts later, though our present cash does not tell us whether we could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tufting crew that better office orders do not mend a missed needle. I would keep the pile sample beside the machine and teach the new operator where to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel and I pay rent from our current wages, but three weeks saved is barely a cushion. A quiet AI future keeps my ordinary job going, which matters more than a faster paperwork screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking pile height after yarn changes and stop for a missed needle. I would ask the mechanic about any AI explanation before adjusting tension, using the printed manual for the setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about our small reserve, though the work itself remains familiar. Regular paid shifts are a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a missed needle look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thin bare stripe appears across the carpet backing. I lift the first tufted strip into the light before we roll a whole length. That small check saves a large amount of wasted yarn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a general AI course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I only use it occasionally to understand a term, and a general class would not teach this needle bar. A paid practical lesson on this floor would be different.

say: I would **keep** sample checks and teach a new operator where to look.
**Office** paperwork does not repair a missed tufting needle.
think: **Current** wages pay rent, but three weeks saved leaves little room.
A **quiet** AI picture preserves useful paid shifts.
do: **Keep** checking pile height and stopping missed-needle runs.
**Check** AI term explanations with the mechanic and printed manual.
feel: **Uneasy** about small savings but relieved by continued work.
S0.quote: I lift the first tufted strip into the light before we roll a whole length.
fieldNote: **Daria** is an experienced average-skill carpet-tufting operator with a vocational textile certificate.

She **uses** AI occasionally for maintenance words, then trusts the mechanic, manual and physical pile samples.

steps.text: Keep sampling tufted carpet and stopping missed-needle runs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor whether office order software is first and what sort of robot is actually planned for the needle line later. I want the machine crew shown a full guarded run before a shift disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot threads and clears the machine, the floor may need fewer hands even though I know the pile checks. Our three weeks saved cannot carry a long hours cut. There are few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a guarded trial and compare bare stripes with our current reject log. If the plant offers paid instruction on a new AI defect screen, I would learn it alongside the mechanic and check its markings against actual carpet. If a local quality job is posted, I would apply only if its net pay after travel and hours cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the rota. I am willing to learn a screen that has been checked on real carpet, not take a robot arm on faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the robot in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch first. I would accept an offered funded paid recognised practical place if a fitter teaches stops and lockout on a safe machine. I cannot learn to clear a robot jam just by watching a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no quality job opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the tufting wage and check the few posted textile jobs within reach. Pay after the fare and shift times must cover rent before I apply. The existence of another plant is not a job offer.

say: I would **ask** for a guarded full run before staffing changes.
**Office** orders change ahead of physical needle-line robotics.
think: A **later** robot may cut tufting hours despite my experience.
**Three** weeks saved and scarce textile jobs leave little room.
do: Request **guarded robot trial**; accept offered recognised funded paid practice only with a fitter, safe stops and lockout.
**Learn** offered AI defect screen on paid time against physical carpet.
Apply for **posted quality work** or textile fallback only if net pay after travel and shifts cover rent.
feel: **Anxious** about roster risk, ready for proven paid instruction.
S1.quote: I cannot learn to clear a robot jam just by watching a trial.
fieldNote: **Daria** requests observation first; robot operation needs an offered funded paid recognised safe-practice place.
She would **actually** learn a new AI defect screen only through paid instruction and physical checks.
A **quality** application and no-vacancy fallback each require real postings, adequate net pay and workable hours.

steps.text: Request guarded needle-line trial and compare bare-stripe rejects
Learn offered AI defect screen on paid time with carpet checks
Apply for posted quality work or textile fallback if net pay/hours after travel cover rent
Accept offered funded paid recognised robot practice with fitter, safe stops and lockout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Joel that AGI may handle the office orders in 2028, but capable robots threading, tufting and clearing jams around 2031 threaten the paid floor shifts. I would ask for written notice before the second change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most tufting hours to go when robots can keep the needle line running themselves. I will be 63 then. Three weeks saved and Joel’s café wage could not cover our rent for long if my pay ended, and I would wake at night counting the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel our planned family celebration and put rent, food and heating on one page. I would ask the landlord about payment timing before a missed rent day and ask the plant for written redeployment terms. I would apply for a posted local carpet-inspection job only with paid supervised machine-safety training and net pay after travel and hours that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the expected loss of the tufting wage. I know how to keep a tufting line running, but I cannot make another mill opening appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children cover bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask them to carry our rent. They have their own homes and expenses. I might ask for a lift to a job interview if one is free, but that is not wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a robot because you know the tufting line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Knowing yarn tension is useful, but I have not learned robot isolation. I would need a funded paid supervised course and a posted paid role before relying on that route. The fitter would have to test me.

say: I would **seek** written notice before capable tufting robots around 2031.
**AGI** office order changes come in 2028 first.
think: **Three** weeks saved and a café wage cannot carry rent for long.
do: **Cancel** family celebration and list essential bills.
**Ask** landlord about timing and plant for redeployment terms.
**Apply** for posted carpet inspection only with paid safe training and bill-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and sleepless rent calculations.
S2.quote: I know how to keep a tufting line running, but I cannot make another mill opening appear.
fieldNote: **Daria** expects hands-on tufting robots to threaten floor wages around 2031, after AGI changes orders.
At 63, her **three-week** reserve and scarce nearby jobs make a large loss hard to absorb.
The **inspection** application requires an actual posting, paid supervised safety training and adequate net income after travel.

steps.text: Cancel planned celebration and list rent heating and food bills
Ask landlord about payment timing before missed rent
Ask plant for written redeployment terms
Apply for posted carpet inspection with paid safety training bill-covering net pay after travel and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time for a paid apprenticeship if the mill wants people to stay. AGI changes orders in 2031; capable robots reach the needle line around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 when those robots arrive. My textile certificate covers this machine, not safe work inside a robot cell. Joel and I hope to retire eventually, but we have not shown income that pays the rent without my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an offered recognised machine-inspection course only if funded on paid shifts, with supervised robot lockout and class hours I can attend. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local inspection job only if net pay after travel and hours cover rent. If no safe paid place opens, I would keep tufting and look for posted textile work at viable wages and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about whether a place will be offered at 66. I can learn alongside a mechanic, but I cannot buy a course while the rent is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the practical test cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mechanic would show me how to stop and isolate the robot arm, then watch me prove it cannot move before clearing a jam. I would want repeated practice on paid time. A robot-safety certificate without a practical isolation test would be paper only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at 66 if it got difficult?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Joel and I had written figures showing retirement income covers rent, food and care costs. We do not have those figures. If they fall short, I would keep seeking paid work.

say: I would **ask** for a funded paid apprenticeship before 2034 robots.
2031 **office** changes arrive before physical needle-line automation.
think: At 66, **textile** experience does not prove robot safety skill.
**Retirement** depends on income that actually covers rent.
do: **Take** offered funded paid recognised course with supervised robot lockout and attendable hours.
**Apply** after training for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and shifts.
If **no** safe course, seek posted textile work with viable wages and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about course availability and rent during learning.
S3.quote: A robot-safety certificate without a practical isolation test would be paper only.
fieldNote: **Daria** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised isolation and workable timing.
**After** qualification she separately applies for a posted local inspection role with sufficient net pay after travel.
**Without** an offered safe place, she retains the tufting wage and checks posted textile jobs.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid recognised course with supervised lockout and attendable shifts
Apply after course for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours
Seek posted textile work if no course and wages and shifts suffice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children ten years gives us time to price retirement and ask for real paid training if I still need a shift. AGI changes orders in 2036 and capable robots reach the tufting line around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 at the first date and 71 at the robot date. We may have stopped paid shifts by then if actual income covers rent, but nothing we have saved now proves it. I will not claim I am still employed in 2039 either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get written retirement-income and household-cost estimates this year. If paid work remains necessary, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot isolation on workable hours, then apply for a posted local inspection role only if net pay after travel and shifts cover our bills. Without that safe course, I would check posted textile work at a bill-covering wage and usable shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the unknown retirement sum. A long warning helps me decide, but it does not give us another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to fund retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They can visit and help us understand paperwork, but they must run their own households. Joel and I need figures for our own rent and income. Family support is kindness, not a number I can assume.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach before leaving the mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a new operator how a missed needle makes a bare stripe across the backing. I would make them lift a strip into the light. A robot will not make a bad carpet saleable.

say: I would **ask** for retirement figures and paid training if work is needed.
think: At 68 in 2036 I **may** have stopped shifts if income covers rent.
At 71 **near** 2039 any factory work depends on actual figures.
do: **Request** written retirement income and household cost estimates.
If **still** working, take offered funded paid supervised course on workable hours.
**After** qualification, apply for posted inspection job only with bill-covering net pay and shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement income and possible work at 71.
S4.quote: A robot will not make a bad carpet saleable.
fieldNote: **Daria** assumes neither a pension payment nor continued mill employment at 71.
If **wages** are needed, her course requires an offered funded paid recognised place with safe practice on workable hours.
An **inspection** application needs a real posting and adequate net pay; without a course she checks viable textile postings.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures
Take offered funded paid recognised course if work needed with supervised isolation and hours
Apply after course for posted inspection job only with bill-covering net pay after travel and shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because tufting robots could take my mill hours around 2031 when we have only three weeks saved. An offered paid practical course and a posted job covering rent would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I still think carpet tufting is learned beside a person who has done it. A thin bare stripe appears across the carpet backing. I would make a new operator look for that before starting a full roll.

headlineQuote: I still think carpet tufting is learned beside a person who has done it.
portrait: **Daria** Ziegler, 58, is an experienced average-skill carpet-tufting operator with a vocational certificate.
She and café **cook** husband Joel rent, have grown children and about three weeks saved on lower operator pay.
She **uses** AI occasionally to explain terms but trusts the mechanic, printed manual and proven practical instruction.
**Few** nearby textile jobs and thin savings make a likely robot shift cut alarming despite her years of work.
She would **take** offered funded paid safe training and seek posted rent-covering work; retirement needs real income figures.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could cut her tufting shifts with three weeks saved and few local alternatives.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised robot training and posted local work with net wages and shifts covering rent.
